findings.description: The pagemap test now accepts `/is not a plain file|EINVAL/`, but with the buffer at `PLAIN_FILE_MAX_BYTES + 8` the EINVAL branch can no longer be reached. In `pagemap_read` (fs/proc/task_mmu.c), the only EINVAL check is that `*ppos` and `count` are both multiples of 8. The first read asks for 1048584 bytes, which is a multiple of 8. Pagemap returns whole 8-byte entries, so after a partial read both the position and `buffer.length - length` stay 8-aligned. So on Linux the read reaches `length === cap + 8` and throws `is not a plain file`. Allowing EINVAL means that if the buffer ever goes back to a size that is not a multiple of 8 (such as the earlier `+ 1`), the test still passes. The function would then never reach its cap path on pagemap, and nothing would notice. Asserting only `'is not a plain file'` would pin the alignment fix. The decision-96 wording "at the cap or on the kernel's refusal" hedges the same way.

The built-in runner patterns still end with `([[:space:]]|$)` (vitest/jest) and `test([[:space:]:]|$)` (package-manager `test`). So the guard still lets through the gap this commit closes for the project's own command. `pnpm test|tail -20`, `npm test;echo done`, `pnpm test>out.log` and `vitest|tail` all pass with exit 0 and run the suite without a slot. Using the same end class, `[[:space:];&|)\`<>]` (plus `:` for the `test` pattern), on both lines would make the guard consistent.

Duplicated Code. The separator class `;&|)\`<>` is now written out twice: in the `end` default at line 532 and in `BARE_COMMAND_END` at line 517. The edit exists to align the two, and nothing ties them together, so a later change to one can drift from the other. The two ends differ on purpose: `BARE_COMMAND_END` also matches `[0-9]+>` and allows optional whitespace first. A shared constant for the separator class would still keep that difference visible. This is a nit because both sets are adjacent in one file and the duplication is small.

The new JSDoc sentence "Throws on any other file, past the cap, or when the kernel refuses the read, as it may refuse a procfs file's before the cap is reached" ends in a dangling possessive ("a procfs file's"), and "any other file" repeats the earlier "only a regular file is read". It could read: "Throws on a non-regular file, on more than the cap, or when the kernel refuses a read (procfs may)."
